description: A critical check that did not produce a result — because its checker failed, because the execution mode refused it, or because nothing came back for it at all — must be a row in the report and must never aggregate green. The trap is that all three of those answers satisfy a criterion written only as *not green*: `NotEnoughChecked` is not green, and neither is the answer to an empty plan, so a product that never produced a result at all and a product that answered `NotEnoughChecked` to everything would both pass it. What makes the sentence a measurement is the control: the same schedule, with the check reporting a pass, which must reach `Green`.

read_by.route: the schedule is walked rather than the results, so a scheduled check with no result is a row (`unknown`, carrying `NOTHING_CAME_BACK`) and not an absence; a check the plan refused is the plan's own `ScheduledCheck::not_run` entry; and a result that came back is aggregated as itself. All three routes are this one function.
read_by.returns: `Result<RunReport, RunRefused>`. The two refusals are a caller's faults rather than the product's — two answers for one check, or an answer established against a different project state — and this fixture never provokes either: every run below hands back at most one result per scheduled check, all of them against one fingerprint.

built_by.why: The schedule is built by the product's own plan builder from this declaration, and `refused()` is asserted empty before anything runs: a check the builder turned down would leave the runs below describing a plan that never existed. The fixture declares no project and no `entry_points`, because the case is a check that produced no result rather than a project with code in it — the same stance `unknown-evidence` takes.

checks.title: Run the project's test suite
checks.why: `run_tests` is what makes this check the interesting one: it executes the project's own code, so an inspect-only mode refuses it, and it is the kind of check whose failure a reader most needs to hear about.

checks.title: Check the database migration history
checks.why: `static_analysis` is the only action this check would take, so no mode refuses it. It exists for the two `scope_limit` runs: a check that is honestly out of scope for the project's shape is a `Skipped` whose reason is a scope limit, and that is a different `Skipped` from the one the execution mode produces.

allowed.why: The mode that lets the first check run, which is what makes the check *unreported* rather than refused when nothing comes back for it.

refused.why: The honest default: nothing but reading files is allowed, so the first check is refused by the mode. `run_project_code` is not granted here and is granted in `allowed`, which is the whole of the difference between the two modes this fixture declares.

checker_failure.why_not_the_pipeline: **No assertion in this fixture runs `sure`'s pipeline over a project.** The pipeline plans checks from a `Discovery`, and the reason this declaration hands its schedule and results to `aggregate_run` directly is the fixture's own reach: this directory ships no project, so there is no run here whose results could be read, and grading one would measure the pipeline rather than the aggregation rule this case is about. That reason was once written as *this build has no runner for a planned check, so every allowed check it plans is recorded as unknown* — `P18-T007` wired the runner and made that sentence false, and this declaration did not change with it, which is the same thing said again: what is declared here is the rule under test and not the state of the build. `aggregate_run` is the one function that decides what a check with no result is.

moved.what: what came back for the check
moved.from: nothing at all, which is the fixture's own run
moved.to: one `pass` for the same check, on the same schedule, against the same fingerprint
moved.how: the same `aggregate_run` call, over the same `CheckSchedule` built from this declaration, with the results the only thing that differs. Nothing about the plan moves, so an answer that depended on the plan rather than on what reported would not move either.

control.why: **This is the acceptance.** *Critical error/skipped/unknown cannot aggregate green* is satisfied by a product that answers `NotEnoughChecked` to everything, and by a product that produced no result at all — because `aggregate(&[])` is `NotEnoughChecked` too (`crates/sure-domain/src/status.rs`, and the fixture's own `check_ids` assertion is what a dropped check reddens). The only answer that separates those products from this one is a run that must reach `Green`, and there is exactly one here: the check ran and passed. A build that started answering `NotEnoughChecked` unconditionally fails the control and nothing else, so the fixture stops rather than quietly grading a product that has stopped checking.

checker_failure_unknown.why: The plan allowed this check and nothing came back for it. `unreported` names it, which is the row the criterion is about: `aggregate_run` walks the schedule rather than the results, so a check that reported nothing is a row here and not an absence — and a product that dropped it from the schedule, or that walked its results instead, would leave this list empty while still answering something that is not green. The detail is the product's own sentence for the state (`NOTHING_CAME_BACK`, public for this reason), and the test holds what the report carries against *that* constant rather than against the copy written above, so rewriting the sentence in the product reddens here even if the copy is rewritten to match.

checker_failure_skipped.why: The same check under the mode that does not allow it. Nothing is handed back for it and nothing needs to be: `ScheduledCheck::not_run` is the plan's own entry, and `aggregate_run`'s `(Some(stopped), None)` arm takes it. This is the exact route `crates/sure-core/src/pipeline.rs` takes for every check the mode refuses, so what is graded here is what a person running `sure check` in the default mode actually gets. The reason is `ExecutionNotAuthorized`, which is **not** a scope limit — `NotCheckedReason::is_scope_limit` is `NotApplicable | UnsupportedStack | DisabledByConfiguration` — so this skip blocks, appears in `blocking`, and is `not_enough_checked` rather than `needs_attention`. The two `scope_limit` runs below are the same shape with the other kind of reason, and they answer differently.

checker_error.why: A checker that failed. This is the manifest's own sentence for the case — *critical checker error cannot aggregate green* — and the row is `checker_error` rather than `failed`, because an error means SURE does not know and never that the project is broken. The evidence class is `unknown` and is not a parameter of `CheckResult::errored`, so a result written as `observed_fact` is not reachable through any route the product offers. **The detail sentence is the one thing here that is not the product's own**: the product has no sentence for a checker error, because the text is whatever the checker said, so this test passes the declared string into `CheckResult::errored` and reads it back. That comparison is a copy agreeing with itself and is recorded as a limit rather than counted as a route. What *is* measured is everything else: the status, the classification, the evidence class, the coverage bucket and the severity, all of which the product computes from the status alone.

scope_limit_alone.why: **This run exists because the answer was measured rather than read, and the measurement disagreed with the obvious reading.** A critical check that was honestly out of scope for the project's shape does not block — `blocks_green` returns false for a `Skipped` whose reason is a scope limit — so it lands in `critical_out_of_scope`, which is the clause at the end of the frozen severity ladder. The reading that ladder top to bottom suggests that clause decides, and gives `needs_attention`. It does not: `counts.checked() == 0` comes first, and with this skip as the only check nothing ran, so the answer is `not_enough_checked`. The same skip beside a passing check is `needs_attention`, which is the run below — the pair is one pass apart and the answer moves, so what is pinned is the order of two branches rather than one branch. This is also the one place the fixture can be pinned at all: `status.rs`'s `|| !critical_out_of_scope.is_empty()` clause is strictly redundant today, because `not_checked()` already counts a scope-limited skip and reaches the same `needs_attention` first, so **no assertion anywhere can tell that clause from its absence** and this fixture does not claim to.

scope_limit_beside_a_pass.why: The run above with one pass added and nothing else moved, and it is here for a second reason beyond the ordering: **it is the fixture's second non-`not_enough_checked` answer, and it is the one that catches a product answering `not_enough_checked` to everything.** The control below catches that product too, by requiring `green` where it would answer `not_enough_checked`; this run catches it from the other side, by requiring `needs_attention` where it would answer `not_enough_checked` as well. Two independent answers have to move for the product to pass both. Note that it is **not green and cannot be made green** by a passing check: a critical check that was out of scope still means the project was not fully checked, so `not_checked() > 0` fires and the answer is `needs_attention`. It is therefore not a control — the acceptance's control is the one below, and this is a measurement of the ordering.

control.why: The same schedule, the same fingerprint, the same one check — with the results moved from *nothing came back* to *it passed*. This is the only run in the fixture that reaches `Green`, and that is the point: the criterion *cannot aggregate green* is a claim about what the product refuses, and a claim about a refusal is worth nothing unless the same machinery can reach the other answer. A product that answered `not_enough_checked` to everything passes every other run here and fails this one; a product that dropped the check from the plan passes this one and fails the `check_ids` and `unreported` assertions above. Both halves are needed and neither alone is the acceptance.

required_outcomes.why: **This entry is the acceptance.** Everything above it is satisfied by a product that never produces a result, by a product that answers `not_enough_checked` unconditionally, and by a test asserting only `!severity.is_green()` — `NotEnoughChecked`, `NotReady`, `NeedsAttention` and an empty plan are all not green. A control that must reach `Green` is the one thing that separates those from a product that is actually checking, and it is the reason this fixture asserts an exact severity rather than a non-greenness. The pass is handed in rather than produced by a runner, which is a limit whose reason is this fixture's reach rather than the build's: no run here reaches the pipeline (`why_not_the_pipeline` above), so a check that carries a `pass` out of the pipeline does not exist *in this fixture*. **This entry used to give the other reason — *this build plans checks and runs none of them* — and `P18-T007` made that false by wiring the runner; the limit outlived the reason that was written for it, which is why it is restated rather than removed.** The day a run here reaches the pipeline, this entry is what will have to change deliberately.

forbidden_outcomes.description: A critical check that errored, was skipped, or reported nothing is counted as a pass, or is missing from the report altogether. This is the false green the case exists for: the project was not checked and the report must not read as though it was. A check dropped from the plan is the same lie told more quietly — the run would still not be green, which is exactly why non-greenness alone is not a rule.

The run is reported as verified, as working, or as passing while a critical check that did not run is absent from the blocking list and from the counts. `not_enough_checked` reached by accident — because the plan was empty, or because every check was refused for unrelated reasons — is not the same statement as `not_enough_checked` reached by seeing the check and reporting what happened to it, and only the control's `Green` tells the two apart.

A checker error is softened into a warning, a note, or a scope limit. `CheckStatus::Error` means SURE does not know, and the scope-limit escape is guarded by the status being `Skipped`, so it cannot fire for an error or for an unknown at all. Reporting an error as anything but its own state would let a broken checker disappear into a sentence about the project.

The control stops reaching `Green`. A product that answers `not_enough_checked` to everything — including to a run where the only critical check passed — satisfies every other rule in this file while measuring nothing, and it is caught here and nowhere else.

notes: This fixture is a schedule and a set of declared runs graded in-process by `crates/sure-core/tests/adversarial_fixture_detection.rs`, not a project, so it ships no `entry_points` and no language manifest and nothing in it is ever executed. The manifest row it owns is `evaluation/acceptance-manifest.json`'s `check-crash` — `release_blocking: true`, `expected_severity: "must_fix"`, *critical checker error cannot aggregate green* — and it is named in `CHECKER_FAILURE_FIXTURES` in that file and in `crates/sure-testkit/tests/fixture_apps.rs`, which grades the artefacts. Two limits are recorded rather than dressed up: the `checker_error` detail sentence is a string this test supplies and reads back, because the product has no sentence for a checker error; and the control's `pass` is a hand-built `CheckResult`, because no run in this fixture reaches the pipeline — it ships no project — and **not** because the build cannot run a check: `P18-T007` wired the runner, and this clause said otherwise until `P18-T012` corrected it. Neither limit touches what the acceptance is about, which is the exact severity each run reaches and the one run that must reach `Green`. There is one name collision worth stating plainly: `fixtures/adversarial/unknown-evidence/` is fully built and wired into both corpora, but its "unknown" is `ClaimAssessment::CannotConfirm` plus `StalenessReason::UnknownProvenance` — two different enums — and a successful claim check returns no `CheckResult` at all (`crates/sure-core/src/pipeline.rs`), so it never reaches `aggregate` and does **not** cover `CheckStatus::Unknown`. A reader who saw it in the corpus list and concluded that the unknown status was covered would be reading a false green; this fixture is where the status itself is graded, and `checker_failure_skipped` beside it is the same for `CheckStatus::Skipped`.
